name: Caroline Bay
description:
Timaru's town beach, a wide sandy bay right below the main street, with lawns, a rose garden, a boardwalk, mini golf and volleyball nets along the back. The big adventure playground is one of the best in the South Island, with a replica lighthouse and shipwreck, and there are barbecues nearby.

It is an easy stop to break up the drive between Christchurch and Dunedin, and a footbridge and underpass link it straight to Stafford Street for food and coffee.
Local tip: Stay into the evening; the penguins come ashore at the southern end of the bay after sunset, a short walk from the playground.
hoursNote: Open any time; playground and toilets on site; paid overnight campervan parking at the southern end

name: Caroline Bay Penguins
description:
Little blue penguins nest in the rocks of the breakwater at the southern end of Caroline Bay, off Marine Parade, and come ashore after dark. It is free to watch, and the area is lit by the port's security lights, so you can see them without torches.

Arrive around dusk and expect to wait about 30 minutes after sunset. Numbers vary from night to night, and some visitors see none, but it is a free alternative to the paid colony in Oamaru. Volunteers are sometimes on hand to explain what is happening.
Local tip: Come between September and March, keep quiet and well back from the rocks, and turn off flash and screen light; the penguins will not come up if they are disturbed.
hoursNote: After sunset; best September to March; no flash, torches or video lights; no dogs in the penguin area in peak season

name: Timaru Botanic Gardens
description:
Large Victorian gardens on the south side of town, with a rose garden, ponds, a rotunda, a glasshouse with a small water feature and bridge, an aviary and a playground. Entry is free.

It is quieter than Caroline Bay and easy to drive through and park wherever you like. Allow an hour or so for a wander.
Local tip: Come in late spring or early summer for the roses, then drive five minutes to Patiti Point for a clifftop walk where seals often lie on the beach.
hoursNote: Listed daily 8am to 8pm; free; parking inside the gardens

name: Te Ana Māori Rock Art Centre
description:
A Ngāi Tahu run centre on George Street near the waterfront, telling the story of the rock art drawn in limestone shelters across South Canterbury and North Otago. There are original drawings preserved behind glass, multimedia displays and a small shop.

Self-guided entry was $22 for adults and $11.50 for children for 2025/26, with guided centre tours at $34. From October to April you can join a guided trip out to a rock art site on farmland, which takes about 3.5 hours and includes some walking over uneven ground.
Local tip: Book the guided centre tour rather than going self-guided; reviewers who went without a guide found the exhibition small for the price.
hoursNote: Listed Tue to Fri 10am to 3.30pm, Sat 9am to 2pm; closed Sun and Mon; site tours October to April

name: South Canterbury Museum
description:
The regional museum, on Perth Street in the centre of town, with two floors on the natural history of the area, Māori and European settlement, shells, butterflies and local collections. Entry is free, with donations welcome.

It is well laid out and the volunteers at the desk are known for being friendly and full of local tips. Some displays are text heavy, but there is plenty to keep kids busy, especially during school holiday events.
Local tip: Weekend opening is afternoons only, so plan a weekday visit if you want a full morning here.
hoursNote: Listed Tue to Fri 10am to 4.30pm, Sat and Sun 1pm to 4.30pm; closed Mondays; free entry

name: Aigantighe Art Gallery
description:
Timaru's public art gallery, set in a 1905 house built for a Scottish farming family who gifted it to the town in 1955. Entry is free. The rooms, fireplaces and old kitchen are kept as they were, so you see the house as well as the art.

The collection runs from historic paintings to contemporary work. Allow about an hour.
Local tip: In winter, look up at the pine trees in the grounds; one is a roosting spot for clusters of monarch butterflies.
hoursNote: Listed Tue to Fri 10am to 4pm, Sat and Sun noon to 4pm; closed Mondays; free entry

name: Curbside Deli
description:
A small sandwich and bagel shop on Stafford Street that bakes its own focaccia, bagels and brioche. The fried chicken sandwiches are the thing to get, especially the chipotle honey, and the toasties and cinnamon scrolls get a lot of love too.

The coffee is good and there are vegetarian options. It is one of the best rated places to eat in Timaru.
Local tip: It is closed Monday and Tuesday and shuts mid-afternoon, so plan it as a lunch stop from Wednesday to Sunday.
hoursNote: Wed to Sat 8.30am to 3pm, Sun 8.30am to 2.30pm; closed Mon and Tue

name: The Grindhouse Cafe
description:
A small, no-fuss coffee spot at the north end of Stafford Street, run by a real coffee enthusiast, with old grindhouse film posters on the walls and seats outside. Locals regularly call it the best coffee in Timaru.

The food is limited to a small cabinet, so treat it as a coffee stop. It is a short walk from Caroline Bay.
Local tip: It opens at 7.15am on weekdays, so it is a good first stop before heading off down the highway.
hoursNote: Mon to Fri 7.15am to 2.30pm, Sat 9am to 2pm; closed Sundays

name: Barker's Foodstore & Eatery
description:
The shop and café of Barker's, the Geraldine company known for fruit syrups, jams and chutneys, on the main street of Geraldine. There are free tasting stations for the syrups (with still or sparkling water), sauces and jams, and you can try the chutneys with your food in the café.

The café does toasties, cakes and good coffee, and the shop is handy for gifts. Geraldine is about 35 minutes north of Timaru, on the way to Tekapo and Mount Cook.
Local tip: Try the syrups with sparkling water before you buy, and walk across the road to the Geraldine Cheese Company while you are here.

name: Geraldine Cheese Company
description:
A small cheesemaker on Geraldine's main street, with the factory visible through a window behind the counter. You can taste around ten of their 30 or so cheeses before buying, from soft cheeses to mozzarella, haloumi and aged cheddars, with small pieces from about $3.

They also scoop ice cream, which makes it a popular road trip stop in summer.
Local tip: Stock up for a picnic or campsite dinner here; prices are reasonable and there are deals if you buy a few.

name: Talbot Forest Scenic Reserve
description:
A patch of old podocarp forest on the edge of Geraldine, a few minutes' walk from the main street, with several short, easy tracks. The tracks run under big old trees, with fantails and birdsong.

The loops are family friendly and can be done in under an hour. There are toilets at the entrance.
Local tip: Walk it after lunch at Barker's; start from Tripp Street and you are back on the main street in under an hour.
hoursNote: Open any time; short easy tracks; toilets at the entrance

name: Caroline Bay Overnight Parking
description:
Council overnight parking for self-contained campervans and caravans right on Caroline Bay, off Marine Parade. It has not been free since December 2024; it is now $20 a night per vehicle, paid through the PayMyPark app, with no bookings.

There are flush toilets, drinking water, a cold outdoor shower and a dump station, and the penguin viewing area is a short walk away. Port noise carries through the night.
Local tip: The paid period runs 9pm to 9am and council staff do move people on after 9am, so be packed up in the morning; bring earplugs for the port.
hoursNote: Certified self-contained only; $20 a night via PayMyPark; 9pm to 9am; max 3 nights; no tents; total fire ban

name: Winchester Bridge Freedom Camping
description:
A free council camping area beside the bridge at Winchester, just off State Highway 1 between Timaru and Geraldine. It is flat and grassy, sheltered from the wind, and open to tents as well as campervans.

There are long drop toilets, picnic tables and a water supply, and it is first come, first served. Road noise is light overnight.
Local tip: It suits a night between Christchurch and Tekapo, since Geraldine and the turn to the Mackenzie Country are about 15 minutes away; the ground can get soft after rain.
hoursNote: Free; tents and campervans; max 3 nights; non-flush toilets, picnic tables, water; first come, first served

name: Te Moana Gorge Camping Area
description:
A free council camping area beside the Te Moana River in the foothills west of Geraldine, open to tents and campervans. There are swimming holes along the river, and further up a pool and a small waterfall that locals jump from.

Facilities are basic: non-flush toilets, picnic tables and walking tracks. There is little or no phone signal. It gets busy over summer holidays and New Year but is often quiet the rest of the year.
Local tip: Save it for summer; the gravel road and the riverside spots get muddy and potholed in winter, so check conditions before driving down to the river.
hoursNote: Free; tents and campervans; non-flush toilets, picnic tables; no water listed; little phone signal; muddy in winter

name: Waitohi Bush Domain
description:
A free council camping area on a hilltop in the countryside west of Temuka, with wide views over Timaru, Pleasant Point and the plains. It is open to tents and campervans, with toilets, a barbecue, picnic tables and a water supply, and short bush walks leading off the site.

It is quiet and roomy, but exposed to wind and weather on top of the hill. Access is by gravel road, and phone signal drops out on the way in.
Local tip: Download directions before you leave town, bring your own toilet paper, and boil the tank water before drinking it.
hoursNote: Free; tents and campervans; toilets, BBQ, water; gravel road; exposed in wind
